dimensions.title: Realistic
dimensions.core_drive: Interest in using tools, working with materials, or caring for tangible things through hands-on work with visible results. Repair, making things, operating equipment, and outdoor work can all involve these activities.
dimensions.positive_value: The appeal of these activities often comes from working directly with something: adjusting a part, testing a material, or getting equipment running again. Notice whether you enjoy making things, troubleshooting, or seeing a tangible result.
dimensions.real_world_cost: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
dimensions.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in working hands-on with tangible things. You could first explore activities involving operating, making, or troubleshooting on site, then compare how different materials, tools, and work settings feel to you.
dimensions.medium_score_reading: Your interest in hands-on activities may depend on what you work with and the setting. Think back to practical problems you willingly took on, and distinguish which parts of making, repairing, or working outdoors appealed to you.
dimensions.low_score_safe_reading: In this response, hands-on activities held relatively limited appeal. This does not mean you lack practical skills. When something specific interests you, a small, safe task can still help you explore further.
work_activity_examples: Assemble or repair a simple object
Make and adjust a physical model
Observe equipment in operation and record anything unusual
Compare how materials differ in practical use
dimensions.common_misread: Realistic interest does not mean strong practical skills, and it does not mean being limited to physical work. Actual skills and training conditions need separate consideration.
dimensions.action_advice: Choose something familiar from the activities below and try operating it or observing it. Afterwards, look back at the part you most wanted to continue.
interest_activity_focus: Using tools and making physical objects
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: working with tools and materials, troubleshooting on site, or turning steps into a visible result?
What training, safety requirements, or resources does this activity involve?
Does the interest remain when the setting or position of responsibility changes?
possible_drains: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
context_costs: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
misread_guardrails: Realistic interest does not mean strong practical skills, and it does not mean being limited to physical work. Actual skills and training conditions need separate consideration.
dimensions.user_visible_boundary: The interpretations below describe interest in activities. Skills, qualifications, and career choices require other information as well.
desktop_insight_by_decile: Your answers suggest very little interest in spending long stretches using tools, working with materials, or repairing equipment. When comparing jobs, distinguish daily on-site operations from occasional equipment use.

Working with parts, assembling things, or maintaining equipment rarely made you want to keep going in these answers. Even in a role that deals with physical objects, ask whether the main responsibility is making things yourself or reviewing plans and coordinating work on site.

Hands-on tasks showed limited appeal in this result. For technical roles, check whether practical work mainly helps you understand equipment and diagnose problems or means taking on installation, maintenance, or fabrication on an ongoing basis.

Operating equipment still holds relatively little appeal in your answers. Compare looking at a sample, trying a tool once, and working at a station every day. Which level of involvement would you want to keep?
Some hands-on tasks interest you. Trying out a new part, figuring out why it does not fit, and repeatedly assembling parts to specification are three different kinds of daily work.

You show some interest in making, troubleshooting, or repairing things. When looking at jobs, notice whether you are more drawn to building something from scratch or getting something that works poorly to run smoothly.

You show a clear interest in hands-on work. When comparing on-site roles, ask how much of a typical week goes to equipment operation, troubleshooting, and maintenance, and which part you would want to do regularly.
Using tools and working with materials appealed to you in this assessment. Look first at roles where you can assemble, adjust, and test things yourself. Ask how much time goes to routine operation.

You showed a clear interest in working regularly with tools, physical objects, or equipment. Operating equipment may focus on keeping it running steadily, while building prototypes may involve repeated changes. Consider which you would want to do over time.

Your answers show strong interest in hands-on work. When screening roles, make building, installing, or fixing things yourself an important criterion. Then compare the location, pace, and on-site requirements.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Your answers show very little interest in making, repairing, or operating things. Even a job centered on equipment can spend most of its time analyzing fault logs or arranging maintenance. On the same production line, one person may inspect the equipment every shift while another checks it in person only when something goes wrong. Consider separately how much hands-on work you want in a job.
examples: Inspect equipment using a checklist
Cut a batch of material to specified dimensions
Keep the same machine running over a shift
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Read one equipment-related job posting and mark which tasks you would do yourself and which you would only need to know the outcome of.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Hands-on activities had relatively little appeal in your answers. You can tighten a loose handle as a favor and see the result in minutes. Spending a week taking parts apart, aligning them, and checking the fit is a different experience. Even if the quick fix appeals to you, consider the volume of repeated manual work separately.
examples: Disassemble a simple mechanism to see how it works
Align a series of identical parts one at a time
Refit spare components in the right order
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Find a full assembly demonstration and notice which stages you would be willing to repeat: setup, assembly, or the final check.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Interest in working directly with objects was relatively low in this result. On-site tasks still vary in how much they ask of you. Trying a new tool takes one run through the process. Maintaining equipment means preparing tools, locating the fault, getting it working again, and doing the same when the next fault occurs. Consider occasional participation and ongoing responsibility separately.
examples: Try a new tool
Look for signs of wear and mark them
Maintain hand tools on a schedule
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask who physically handled the most recent equipment fault and how often that kind of work comes up.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Hands-on tasks attracted relatively little interest this time. If you do want to try one, the appeal might be solving a specific problem and seeing what changed. Tightening a cardboard fastener until it stops wobbling and cutting twenty matching pieces both involve working with your hands. In the second case, the result you see is consistency.
examples: Adjust a cardboard fastener
Cut a batch of material along marked lines
Check the gaps after fitting the parts
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Choose a safe, small adjustment to a household item. After the fix, notice whether you want to try another version.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Some hands-on tasks appeal to you. Putting something together for the first time leaves room for exploration and trial and error. Getting a known procedure to work consistently takes repetition. Even on one prototype, you might be drawn to a particular part of the process, such as building from a drawing, adjusting the fit, or trying out the finished piece.
examples: Build a cardboard model
Adjust the fit between two parts
Assemble the same item repeatedly to a specification
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Compare a one-off build with repeated assembly and note which you would want to do routinely.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Hands-on work had some appeal in your answers. If a cart won't steer smoothly, you might want to see what moving a wheel changes. With a sketch in front of you, you might want to make something usable from it. Troubleshooting and prototyping call for different tools and take up different parts of a working week.
examples: Test a structure using physical materials
Find where a small mechanism catches
Try a part after an adjustment
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Compare one prototyping job and one repair job. Look at what each handles and delivers in a typical week.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Making, repairing, or working on-site had some appeal in your answers. Technical jobs can split hands-on work and judgment among different people. One person operates at preset settings, someone else repeatedly fits and adjusts parts, and another checks the finished result. If you like verifying the outcome yourself, find out which part you would own.
examples: Measure a sample against its specifications
Test-fit parts and adjust their position
Verify a finished product using a physical sample
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask what happened the last time a test fit failed, who could change it on the spot, and who only recorded the result.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Working with physical objects had a fairly strong appeal in your answers. When you move a hole or try a different joint in a sample, you can quickly tell whether the change helped. Some technical jobs allow this kind of back-and-forth testing. In others you mainly use equipment somebody else has set up. Find out how much you would get to change yourself.
examples: Build a sample from a sketch
Change a joint and test how it fits
Compare two samples under a real load
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Start with jobs that include hands-on prototyping. Check the tools, training, and working conditions.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Your answers show a clear interest in regular work with tools and physical objects. Making something gives you the moment it takes shape. A repair makes something usable again. Operating equipment lets you see it complete a task reliably. Consider which result would make you want to do the next job.
examples: Make a sample using hand tools
Locate and replace a faulty part
Adjust equipment based on its readings
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask someone in the field to describe a recent physical deliverable and say where they worked hands-on and where they worked with others.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: You're strongly drawn to working directly with physical objects. Make hands-on building, adjustment, or maintenance a priority when comparing jobs, then look at where and how you would do it. Precision assembly at a bench, urgent repair on-site, and repeated prototype builds all have visible outcomes. The space, shifts, and freedom to make adjustments will shape what your week actually looks like.
examples: Assemble fine components at a workbench
Test a more reliable design with a prototype
Check that equipment runs after maintenance
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Pick two hands-on jobs and compare the tasks, conditions, and training requirements of a typical shift.

desktop_focus_by_band.low: Hands-on tasks held limited appeal in these answers, even if they ranked among your leading interests. The scene below can help you identify a practical task you would be willing to do occasionally.
desktop_focus_by_band.medium: Start with work where you can see a physical change, then consider how often you would want to be the person making it happen.
desktop_focus_by_band.high: Start with roles where you regularly handle physical objects, test things in person, or make adjustments on site. Working with your hands to verify a result is worth looking for.

dimensions.title: Investigative
dimensions.core_drive: Interest in asking questions, gathering evidence, and analyzing causes to understand why things work as they do. Reading research material, comparing explanations, and testing hypotheses are typical activities.
dimensions.positive_value: The appeal may lie in the question itself or in the process of checking evidence and reasoning. Notice whether you want to investigate inconsistencies, revise explanations, and keep exploring when there is no conclusion yet.
dimensions.real_world_cost: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
dimensions.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in analysis and inquiry. You could first try looking up information, comparing evidence, or explaining a phenomenon, and observe which questions you want to explore in depth.
dimensions.medium_score_reading: You may want to investigate some topics in depth while preferring a quick, practical conclusion for others. Looking at specific questions and past experiences is more useful than labeling yourself as someone who loves research.
dimensions.low_score_safe_reading: In this response, sustained inquiry and abstract analysis held relatively limited appeal. This does not mean lower understanding or learning ability, and it does not prevent you from using analytical methods when needed.
work_activity_examples: Turn a vague question into one that can be checked against evidence
Compare information from different sources
Propose different explanations for the same phenomenon
Design observations that distinguish between explanations
dimensions.common_misread: Interest in research is distinct from intelligence, subject knowledge, and research skills. The score cannot demonstrate these abilities or determine a specific field of study.
dimensions.action_advice: Choose a question you are curious about. Start with a question, evidence-checking, or hypothesis activity below, then look back at the step that most interested you.
validation_questions: Do I want to spend time checking evidence, modeling, and comparing evidence, or do I mainly want a quick answer?
What training, data access, or professional background does this question require?
When there is no clear answer, do I want to keep asking questions or move on to carrying something out?
possible_drains: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
context_costs: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
misread_guardrails: Interest in research is distinct from intelligence, subject knowledge, and research skills. The score cannot demonstrate these abilities or determine a specific field of study.
dimensions.user_visible_boundary: The interpretations below describe interest in activities. Skills, qualifications, and career choices require other information as well.
desktop_insight_by_decile: Spending long periods looking up information, comparing explanations, or testing them repeatedly rarely appealed to you in this assessment. Ask whether investigation is an occasional step before delivery or a task you would do every day.

Investigating causes held relatively little appeal in these answers. Some roles ask you to make sense of someone else's analysis, while others involve gathering the evidence yourself. Those are different kinds of work.

Your answers suggest relatively little interest in sustained investigation. When looking at analytical roles, distinguish checking a few existing sources from investigating an open question from the ground up.

Research tasks still show limited appeal in this result. If a practical problem makes you want to look deeper, notice whether you want a quick confirmation or would also enjoy comparing several explanations.
Some questions may make you want to know what caused the problem. Distinguish checking the facts in front of you from working out which explanation those facts support.
You show some interest in gathering information and analyzing causes. If a conclusion is unclear, notice whether you want to look for new evidence or make better sense of what you already have.

Your answers show a clear interest in finding out what caused a problem. Ask whether the findings usually explain an event, change a proposed solution, or determine whether the investigation should continue.

You showed considerable interest in asking questions, comparing sources, and testing explanations. Look first at work where you can access the original data and revise your judgment in light of new findings.

Your answers show a clear interest in getting to the cause and checking the evidence. Ask whether you can frame the question and assess evidence yourself or mainly produce reports using established definitions.

Moving from a vague observation to an explanation you can verify strongly appealed to you. When exploring research roles, consider the topic, whether you help design the tests, and whether the evidence can shape what happens next.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Repeatedly gathering evidence and explaining what happened had very little appeal this time. Research can mean reading conflicting sources, finding a gap in the evidence, and going back to check it. Many other jobs use existing findings to move a task forward. When comparing roles, distinguish using a conclusion from owning the investigation.
examples: Gather different versions of the same information
Verify where each claim came from
Make an additional observation to test an explanation
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Check whether “analysis” in a job posting means reviewing findings that already exist or starting an investigation yourself.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Investigating causes and rechecking evidence had relatively little appeal this time. If a number is wrong, you might still check the source sheet so you can deliver. A deeper investigation asks why the discrepancy keeps happening, and the first batch of evidence may not settle it. Ask where an investigation usually ends in each job.
examples: Spot-check an unusual number
Find the original source of a record
Check whether a discrepancy keeps recurring
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask the team to describe a recent investigation and how long it needed follow-up, from an hour to several days.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Extended investigation attracted little interest in your answers. To make a particular decision, finding one missing fact might be enough. Research often asks you to seek evidence that can separate several plausible explanations. Consider how much of that checking process you would want to own.
examples: Verify a fact from available records
List two explanations for one observation
Look for evidence that could rule one explanation out
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Think of a question you recently looked up. Identify whether you were drawn to the answer, the process of finding the cause, or both.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: A lengthy analysis process had relatively little appeal this time. A concrete question, such as why enrollment dropped, may still make you want to dig. Reading the summary, checking one piece of evidence, and designing an investigation all take a different level of involvement. When several jobs mention research, find out which of those they hand to you.
examples: Read a summary of possible causes
Check the figures behind one claim
Use interviews to distinguish two explanations
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Compare two jobs by how often you would have to pose a question yourself and how much material you would personally check.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: You have some interest in getting to the bottom of specific questions. When two data sets disagree, checking how the figures were recorded may settle it. If it doesn't, you can start looking for what changed. Think about whether you find satisfaction in establishing the facts, explaining them, or both.
examples: Check how two sets of figures were defined
Mark the differences that remain after recalculation
List factors that could explain the change
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Work through one familiar discrepancy. Once you have confirmed the facts, notice whether you still want to know more.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Analytical tasks had some appeal this time. When only one data set supports a claim, you might want to find another source to check it. You might be more drawn to taking scattered clues and building an explanation others can verify. When you compare jobs, think about whether you want to spend more time gathering evidence or working out what it means.
examples: Find an independent source for a claim
Sort scattered clues into groups
Explain what a set of interacting data points suggests
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Read a public research memo and pick out the part of the work you would want to take on.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Understanding why things happen had some appeal in your answers. If customers leave at the same step, one analysis job may update the same report each week. Another may investigate why people leave and propose a change to test. Access to raw evidence, room to frame the question, and what the team does with your findings shape the daily work.
examples: Plot when a problem occurs
Cross-check interviews against behavior records
Propose a change worth testing
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask what the team's latest analysis changed and who generally starts the investigation.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Checking evidence and comparing explanations were fairly appealing in your answers. A change in records, procedures, or conditions could each explain the same exception, and each calls for a different check. Narrowing the possibilities can be satisfying. You may still need to explain what is known so far while waiting for missing evidence.
examples: Map the evidence for several explanations
Find a condition you can check for each explanation
Distinguish open questions from findings so far
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Check whether a role gives you access to raw data and time to investigate. Ask what you deliver when the answer is still uncertain.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Your answers show a clear interest in asking why. Two stores run the same promotion and get different results. You might check the location, inventory, and execution one by one to see what evidence would overturn the initial explanation. A job that mainly updates the figures gives you fewer chances to do that deeper work.
examples: Propose a testable explanation for an anomaly
Test your reasoning against another set of evidence
Revise a finding in light of a counterexample
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: When evidence last challenged the team's view, ask whether someone in this role could investigate further and revise the conclusion.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Exploring and testing explanations strongly appealed to you. Research can start with a vague question, require a choice of method, and end with a candid account of what the evidence can support and how others can repeat the key checks. Alongside the subject itself, consider whether you can frame the question, design the check, and use the findings to decide what comes next.
examples: Turn a vague question into one you can test
Design a comparison that distinguishes possible causes
Record the limits of the evidence and how to verify it
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask how two research roles frame questions, access source material, and use findings. Ask each team for a specific project example.

desktop_focus_by_band.low: Research can rank high in this profile while still holding limited appeal. Start with roles that use a small amount of research to solve an immediate problem.
desktop_focus_by_band.medium: Questions and evidence are among the more appealing parts of this profile. Consider how much of your week you would want to spend investigating, beyond the research needed for an immediate task.
desktop_focus_by_band.high: Checking explanations and tracing causes stood out in your answers. Look first at roles where you can work with firsthand information and help draw the conclusions.

dimensions.title: Artistic
dimensions.core_drive: Interest in creating, expressing ideas, and exploring different forms by turning ideas into writing, images, sound, or performance. These activities usually allow multiple forms of expression rather than one standard answer.
dimensions.positive_value: The appeal may lie in developing a new angle, choosing a style, or repeatedly refining a piece of work. Distinguish whether you prefer creating freely, communicating to an audience, or improving existing content.
dimensions.real_world_cost: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
dimensions.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in creating and expressing ideas. You could first try different media, such as writing, visuals, or sound, and compare which forms you want to keep refining.
dimensions.medium_score_reading: Your interest in expression may center on particular media or topics. Start with your experience and distinguish whether you enjoy developing ideas, making work, or appreciating it. You do not need to be interested in every artistic activity.
dimensions.low_score_safe_reading: In this response, open-ended creative work held relatively limited appeal. This does not mean a lack of creativity or aesthetic appreciation, and it does not rule out enjoying a particular form of expression.
work_activity_examples: Develop different ways to express the same topic
Turn complex information into an explanatory diagram
Write, take photographs, or make a sound piece
Revise the structure and style of a piece of work in response to feedback
dimensions.common_misread: The Artistic score reflects interest in creative activities. It does not evaluate the quality of your work, your creativity, or your aesthetic ability.
dimensions.action_advice: Choose a form of expression below and finish a small piece of work. Then look back at whether you want to revise it and what you would change.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: developing ideas, choosing a style, refining versions, or adjusting after feedback?
What training, tools, aesthetic standards, or conditions for collaboration does this task require?
When the work is evaluated, does my interest grow, weaken, or shift to another part of the activity?
possible_drains: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
context_costs: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
misread_guardrails: The Artistic score reflects interest in creative activities. It does not evaluate the quality of your work, your creativity, or your aesthetic ability.
dimensions.user_visible_boundary: The interpretations below describe interest in activities. Skills, qualifications, and career choices require other information as well.
desktop_insight_by_decile: Tasks that involve regularly coming up with new material or refining how it is presented held very little appeal in this assessment. Ask how much time goes to starting from scratch, revising drafts, and delivering to a set standard.

Trying out styles and repeatedly revising a piece rarely appealed to you in these answers. For a role with creative responsibilities, ask whether you occasionally contribute ideas or take work from concept to final draft every week.

Creating and expressing ideas held relatively little appeal in this result. When comparing roles, see whether you feel differently about commenting on finished work, trying a way to present something, and shaping the direction of a piece over time.

Open-ended brainstorming and refining creative work held relatively little appeal in these answers. If particular content catches your interest, ask whether the topic itself draws you in or whether you would spend time finding a distinctive way to tell the story.
Some tasks involving expression may appeal to you. Given the same material, consider whether you would most enjoy explaining it clearly, trying several styles, or refining one version until it works.
You show some interest in creating work and expressing ideas. Compare what appeals to you about coming up with a new subject, choosing how to present it, and revising an existing piece.
Creative work had some weight in these answers. In a content or design role, see which decisions you would own from concept through delivery, especially what you can still change after feedback.

You showed considerable interest in choosing how to present ideas and trying out different versions. Look first at roles that involve shaping and revising the work. Ask whether you deliver to a fixed style or can propose a different approach.

Developing ideas, expressing them, and refining their presentation showed clear appeal in your answers. Ask who sets the content direction, who chooses the form, and how much time is left to try drafts and revise them.

You show strong interest in creating and expressing ideas on an ongoing basis. When assessing roles, make freedom to choose the form and lead revisions important criteria. Then compare creative freedom, pace of delivery, and review requirements.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Developing work, choosing its style, and revising it had little appeal in your answers. A job may still ask you to make information clearer now and then. Finding an image for existing material leaves you with a few decisions. Setting the direction of a piece takes repeated trials and choices. Ask how often you would handle that kind of open-ended work.
examples: Arrange a page in an existing layout
Replace an illustration that is hard to read
Check the final draft against a checklist
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Look at something the team actually delivered. Find out who shapes the initial idea and who makes revisions.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Sustained creative work held relatively little appeal this time. Swapping out an example to explain something is one commitment. Finding a fresh way to cover similar subjects every week is another. For content jobs, ask how much work is explaining clearly, following an established brief, or deciding what each new piece should cover.
examples: Change an example in an existing draft
Choose illustrations in a fixed style
Try a new opening on an existing subject
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask for a typical content brief and see how much of the subject and format is already set when it reaches you.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Open-ended expression drew relatively little interest this time. On a creative project, you could point out where two drafts are confusing, refine the details of one of them, or propose two approaches from scratch. A subject can draw you in on its own. Consider whether shaping how it is expressed also appeals to you.
examples: Mark what a reader could misinterpret in two drafts
Replace a title with a clearer one
Try rewriting a passage from a draft
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Find out whether the job is about making focused changes to an existing piece or starting regularly from a blank page.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Coming up with ideas from scratch had relatively little appeal. You might still enjoy reframing a subject you care about, particularly when you know the goal, audience, and length. When comparing roles, consider both creating within a clear brief and regularly producing drafts without an established direction.
examples: Switch to an example a beginner would recognize
Rearrange a page within a fixed layout
Write two possible openings to one passage
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Use the same material to make a small revision and to try an idea from scratch. Notice which you would keep doing.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Some kinds of expression appeal to you. With the same story, you can spend your time finding the right angle or adjusting the pace so readers can follow it. Revising part of a piece and making those choices throughout a project can be satisfying in different ways. Think about which part would make you want to do another version.
examples: Change the sequence of a story
Turn a short passage into a three-panel drawing
Try two openings and pick one
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Recall two pieces you willingly revised. Identify the specific problem you wanted to solve in each.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Creative work had some appeal in your answers. You can begin with a new angle on a topic or with a form, testing how sound, image, and text work together. Some roles mostly produce work in an established style, while others allow room to try ideas. Find out which version of the day-to-day work would interest you.
examples: Write a short piece inspired by a photo
Choose different images for the same instructions
Compare the pace of a piece before and after editing
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Pick two comparable pieces and ask a practitioner which creative choices they personally made.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: You showed some interest in developing and refining how something is expressed. On some jobs a round of feedback means implementing each requested change. On others you can come up with a different approach to solve the underlying problem. Ask who makes those calls and who signs off on the finished piece.
examples: Turn feedback into a design question
Try two layouts for the same problem
Compare how readers move through a piece before and after a change
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask how much freedom someone in this role had to try a new approach on the latest round of revisions.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Choosing a form and revising a piece were fairly appealing this time. The same topic could open with a person, a sound, or a telling detail. That choice affects what the audience understands first. A job might set firm brand requirements and leave room to experiment within them. Ask how much of that room is yours to use.
examples: Design two openings on the same subject
Tell one story with images and again with sound
Adjust the pace in response to an audience
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Ask the team to walk you through a piece from concept to release and identify which creative decisions belong to the role.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Your answers show a clear interest in creative work. You might enjoy deciding what people see first and remember afterward, or revising a piece until it has the intended effect. Concept work, finishing a piece, and carrying forward someone's existing style are all called design. They leave different amounts of room for choices and revisions.
examples: Try two narrative sequences for an exhibition
Develop a visual style from a rough sketch
Use feedback to decide what to leave out or leave unsaid
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Compare creative authority, number of revision rounds, and deadlines. Ask who is responsible for the finished work.

desktop_atlas_by_decile.reading: Developing and expressing ideas strongly appealed to you. Creative freedom can come from choosing the subject, choosing a medium, or shaping the pace of the work. Real assignments also have an audience, a budget, and feedback to handle. Use the creative decision you most want to make as a criterion when comparing jobs.
examples: Invent a new form for an existing theme
Rework the same piece in a different medium
Keep refining a narrative in response to feedback
desktop_atlas_by_decile.next_step: Examine real work from two creative roles. Check which decisions each one owns and which production constraints it has to work within.
